findings.quote: Given the fluctuations in the property and money markets there is a risk of some adverse revenue impact when the override is removed and consequently the Council holds an earmarked reserve against this risk.

findings.headline: Council will require external borrowing to meet future capital expenditure
findings.detail: The council has avoided external General Fund borrowing by financing capital projects through internal cash resources. However, the report explicitly signals that external borrowing will be necessary in future to meet capital expenditure requirements. Currently all external debt (£288.526m) is Housing Revenue Account-related.
findings.matters: Marks a change from the current position and indicates future demand for credit market access, relevant to lender appetite and covenant headroom
findings.figures: £288.526m external borrowing (HRA-only); no General Fund external borrowing taken in last two years
findings.quote: However external borrowing will be necessary in the future to meet its capital expenditure requirements, and more external borrowing,.

findings.headline: HRA is ring-fenced with no general fund backup; the council explicitly warns of account collapse if balance is not maintained
findings.detail: The HRA must finance its activities entirely from the rental income it generates, with no access to general fund reserves. The report explicitly states that failure to maintain a positive balance would lead to HRA collapse at the council.
findings.matters: For a lender, this means there is no municipal safety net if the HRA encounters financial difficulty. The HRA must remain solvent through its own revenue alone.
findings.figures: Ring-fenced account with no general fund subsidy available
findings.quote: The HRA is a ring-fenced account and is required to finance its activities from the income it generates - predominantly rental income. Failure to maintain a positive balance of the HRA account would lead to the collapse of the HRA at Oxford City Council.

findings.headline: 63% of HRA tenants (5,115 of 8,077) depend on Housing Benefit or Universal Credit, creating policy risk to rental income
findings.detail: The HRA's rental income is highly dependent on government benefit policy. The majority of tenants rely on Housing Benefit or Universal Credit housing costs to pay rents. Changes to Local Housing Allowance rates or benefit eligibility would reduce HRA income independent of council action.
findings.matters: For a lender, this represents policy risk to revenue forecasts. Government decisions on benefit rates or caps could reduce HRA income materially and unpredictably.
findings.figures: 5,115 tenants claiming benefits as at end September 2025: 1,316 Housing Benefit, 3,799 Universal Credit; 63% of 8,077 total
findings.quote: As at the end of September 2025 there were a total of 5,115 HRA tenants (63%) claiming Housing Benefit or the Housing Cost element of Universal Credit

findings.headline: £4.024 million annual rental income is foregone on 98% of the existing stock due to rents being capped below formula rent
findings.detail: 7,986 of the HRA's 8,077 properties have rents below the formula rent that government policy prescribes. This arose from historical rent caps (2023/24 capped at 7% when CPI was 10.1%) and creates structural income loss that cannot easily be recovered as rents can only be moved toward formula rent on re-let following vacancy.
findings.matters: Unrecoverable foregone income weakens the HRA's revenue base and its ability to fund capital investment and maintain services without maximum annual increases.
findings.figures: 7,986 properties of 8,077 total; £4,024,020 annual rental income foregone; £77,385 weekly
findings.quote: Actual Rent is less than Formula Rent 7,986 £77,385 £4,024,020

findings.headline: Strategic review identified 10-year financial challenges requiring maximum rent increases to remain viable
findings.detail: External consultants conducting a 2024/25 HRA Strategic Review found that the HRA faces a challenging financial future within the next 10 years due to investment demands from new legislation and housing standards. The council states it needs to maximize income streams to remain viable and warns that a rent increase lower than inflation would create an unsustainable position with risk of failing tenants in service provision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand if an HRA has structural financial problems ahead and whether rental income will be sufficient to fund obligations without general fund subsidy.
findings.figures: 10-year outlook; £4.024m annual rental income currently foregone on existing stock
findings.quote: A HRA Strategic Review undertaken by external consultants during 2024/25 identified that the HRA faced a challenging financial future within the next 10 years due to the scale of investment required because of the demands placed on it by new legislation and housing standards.

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Blackbird Leys Regeneration site start delayed to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027, pushing delivery 6+ months later
findings.detail: The GF element of this major regeneration project is forecast to slip by £0.19m in 2025/26. 'Anticipated date to start on site for shell and core now slipped to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027.' This represents a material delay to a flagship capital project.
findings.matters: Major regeneration projects are bellwethers for a council's execution capability and often underpin economic development strategy. A 6+ month delay suggests either planning/approvals challenges or delivery partner issues. For housing-heavy councils, delays to major housing developments affect long-term borrowing assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.19m slippage for GF element of Blackbird Leys Regeneration; site start now October/November 2025, completion March 2027
findings.quote: Blackbird Leys Regenerations (GF element) - £0.19m slippage forecast for 2025/26. Anticipated date to start on site for shell and core now slipped to October/November 2025 with completion now predicted for March 2027

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: ODS Fleet Replacement Programme slipped by £1.744m (30% of budget) due to procurement delays, rolling into 2026/27 with no certainty on timing
findings.detail: The £1.744m slippage represents 30% of the budgeted fleet replacement spend. The report states 'A full review of the procurement process has delayed ordering new assets' and 'Much of the asset procurement is expected to roll over into 2026/27.' This is a material capital project with execution risk.
findings.matters: Fleet replacement is essential for service delivery (ODS is the council's parking and waste services company). A 30% slip suggests procurement challenges or market supply issues. For a lender, capital project slippages indicate execution risk and potential knock-on delays to other programmes.
findings.figures: £1.744m slippage (30% of ODS Fleet budget); forecast to roll into 2026/27
findings.quote: ODS Fleet Replacement Programme – a slippage of £1.744m (30% of the budget) is forecast. A full review of the procurement process has delayed ordering new assets and informed this latest forecast. Much of the asset procurement is expected to roll over into 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Revenue Service printing and postage costs overrunning by £0.250m despite decentralisation efforts, with no fix until 2026/27
findings.detail: Revenues and Benefits expected to overspend by £0.292m, of which £0.250k (actually £0.250m based on context) is from printing, postage and carriage costs for council tax and business rates billing. The council decentralised the printing budget from the corporate print room, but this 'insufficient to cover printing and postage costs', and reductions 'are planned although these savings will materialise from 2026-27 onwards'—a full year or more away.
findings.matters: This suggests a failed cost-control initiative; decentralisation was supposed to control costs but made them worse. The delay in fixing it (to 2026/27) means the council is absorbing a controllable overspend for a further year. It signals execution and procurement challenges.
findings.figures: £0.250m printing and postage overspend (revenues service); £0.292m total Revenues and Benefits adverse variance
findings.quote: Decentralisation of the printing and postage budget from corporate print room is insufficient to cover printing and postage costs for the Revenues Service. Reductions in printing costs associated with the annual billing of business rates and council tax are planned although these savings will materialise from 2026-27 onwards

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 compliance has been elevated to a red corporate risk, explicitly identifying potential for major tenant safety incidents, regulatory intervention, and reputational damage
findings.detail: This risk was reclassified from amber in Q1 to red in Q2. The report states the risk 'evaluates the potential impact if the Council, in its capacity as a landlord, fails to fully comply with the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 customer standards, particularly the Safety and Quality Consumer Standard', and notes that failure could result in 'a major incident that compromises tenant safety, leading to sanctions, regulatory intervention, and severe reputational damage.'
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention in housing is a serious reputational and operational threat. For a council that is a major landlord, regulator sanctions could constrain borrowing, trigger intervention, or require capital spending to remediate compliance failures. This moved from amber to red in one quarter, suggesting deterioration.
findings.figures: 1 red risk escalation in Q2 2025/26 (Social Housing Act); 6 red risks, 8 amber risks total
findings.quote: A failure to meet Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 customer/consumer standards – this risk has been reclassified from an amber risk in 1Q to a red risk in 2Q... Such a failure could result in a major incident that compromises tenant safety, leading to sanctions, regulatory intervention, and severe reputational damage

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: HRA housing acquisitions delayed, creating £0.264m shortfall in dwelling rent income year to date and £0.220m further pressure at year-end
findings.detail: The council's new home acquisitions—a core revenue driver for the HRA—are running behind schedule. Year-to-date, dwelling rent is underachieving by £0.264m specifically due to 'the timings of the acquisition of new homes', with a further £0.220m pressure forecast from 'delayed acquisitions' by year-end. This directly erodes the HRA's revenue position.
findings.matters: Rental income is fundamental to HRA stability and the council's housing strategy. Delays in acquisitions suggest either capital constraints or market challenges; either way, housing supply targets are slipping, which matters to lenders evaluating the council's ability to deliver its development programme.
findings.figures: £0.264m dwelling rent underachievement YTD from delayed acquisitions; £0.220m forecast pressure at year-end from delayed acquisitions
findings.quote: Dwelling rent underachieving by £0.264m due to the timings of the acquisition of new homes which generate rental income... pressures on dwelling rent of £0.220m arising from delayed acquisitions

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: Housing benefits expenditure forecast to overspend by £1.5m due to inability to claim subsidy on supported housing—a structural, uncontrollable cost
findings.detail: The council explicitly notes a £1.5m increase in net housing benefits costs expected at year-end, with supported housing benefit expenditure continuing to rise. The underlying problem is the council's inability to claim subsidy on supported housing accommodation benefit expenditure, and the council states it is 'actively working on mitigations' but acknowledges the situation is being 'monitored'—language suggesting no immediate fix exists.
findings.matters: Housing benefits are demand-driven and difficult to control; this cost is being borne by the council rather than funded through subsidy. For a lender, this signals uncontrollable expenditure growth driven by factors outside council management (homelessness, supported housing demand), a red flag for budget stability.
findings.figures: £1.5m increase in net cost of housing benefits; supported housing benefit expenditure continues to rise with no subsidy recovery available
findings.quote: current indications suggest that this will be offset by a £1.5m increase in the net cost of housing benefits payments as supported housing benefit expenditure continues to rise. The council is actively working on mitigations to try and contain overspends largely arising from the inability to claim subsidy on supported housing accommodation benefit expenditure

findings.paper_title: Q2 integrated performance report 2526 DRAFT v2.0
findings.headline: General Fund adverse variance of £0.641m is sticky and unchanged from Q1, with major pressures in staffing and support service costs
findings.detail: The adverse variance remains almost static compared to Q1's £0.656m forecast, indicating structural budget pressures rather than one-time items. Law, Governance & Strategy faces £0.462m adverse variance from staff recruitment difficulties and locum dependency; Financial Services £0.758m from salary cost pressures and revenue service printing costs; Information & Technology £0.7m including £0.5m cyber incident response.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends across multiple services suggest underlying cost control challenges, and repeated salary/staffing pressures indicate difficulty recruiting and retaining staff—a marker of operational stress in key support functions.
findings.figures: General Fund adverse variance £0.641m (Q1: £0.656m); Law/Governance £0.462m adverse; Financial Services £0.758m adverse; Information & Technology £0.7m adverse
findings.quote: The overall Net Budget Requirement for 2025/26 agreed by the Council in February 2025 was £30.25m... At 2Q there is an adverse projected 2025/26 outturn variance of £0.641m compared to the 2025/26 latest budget... almost static to the forecast adverse variance of £0.656m reported at 1Q

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan provides for complete exhaustion of risk reserve to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The MTFP plans to exhaust the council's £6.690m risk reserve entirely and spend half of the £10.406m direct revenue funding reserve to finance the capital programme. This eliminates the council's contingency buffer for unexpected financial pressures.
findings.matters: Planned depletion of reserves to zero removes financial resilience for future shocks and limits capacity to respond to emergencies or changed circumstances.
findings.figures: Risk reserve £6.690m; direct funding reserve £10.406m
findings.quote: The current MTFP provides for exhausting the risk reserve and spending half of the direct funding reserve to fund capital

findings.headline: HRA repairs costs £7.82m over budget due to new Housing Regulator compliance standards
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account repairs overspent by £7.82m on £20.38m spend, driven by new compliance standards from the Housing Regulator requiring increased fire safety (£1.145m), asbestos clearance and surveys, and electrical upgrades on 5-year cycle (£0.724m). The council describes this as an "exceptional year" but has increased 2025/26 budgets to accommodate ongoing compliance costs.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs are non-negotiable and recurring; budgets were insufficient and higher baseline spending will continue, reducing capacity for other investment.
findings.figures: £7.82m overspend; fire safety £1.145m; electrical upgrades £0.724m
findings.quote: The 2024/25 overspend for repairs is due to an exceptional year following the introduction of significant changes to the compliance standards set by the Housing Regulator. Notable areas in respect of this are Fire Safety, Asbestos and Electrical Upgrades / Inspections.

findings.headline: Housing benefit costs will increase from 1 April 2025 due to Universal Credit transfer, beyond council control
findings.detail: Housing benefit costs overspent by £1.491m in 2024/25. The council explicitly signals that working age claimants transferring to Universal Credit from 1 April 2025 will worsen this pressure. The council notes the service is largely commissioned outside its control by NHS, Oxfordshire County Council and other districts.
findings.matters: A policy-driven cost increase beyond the council's control is imminent, constraining the ability to manage this budget line in future years.
findings.figures: £1.491m overspend 2024/25
findings.quote: There will be an increased impact from 1 April 2025 as a result of working age housing benefit claimants being transferred to Universal Credit.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £1.89m with £1.73m annual pressure embedded in forward budget
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation overspent by £1.89m in 2024/25 due to ongoing demand. The council has built a permanent £1.73m annual pressure into the 2025/26 budget and MTFP, indicating this demand is expected to persist as a structural cost.
findings.matters: Growing demand-led costs are difficult to control once embedded in budgets and signal housing market stress beyond the council's capacity to manage.
findings.figures: £1.89m overspend 2024/25; £1.73m annual structural pressure
findings.quote: Due to the ongoing TA demand the 2024-25 actual overspend is £1.89m. An annual pressure of £1.73m has been included in the base budget within the 2025-26 budget and ongoing MTFP to address the ongoing demand for this category of accommodation.

findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £1.549m requires transfer from risk reserve to balance
findings.detail: The council's operational spending exceeded revenue by £1.549m in 2024/25, forcing a drawdown from the risk reserve to balance the General Fund. This represents 5.4% of the council's £28.604m net budget requirement and signals the operating account is not covering costs.
findings.matters: Reserve transfers mask structural budget gaps and reduce financial flexibility for unexpected pressures in future years.
findings.figures: £1.549m deficit; £28.604m net budget requirement
findings.quote: deficit of £1.549 million ("m") before a recommended equivalent transfer from risk reserves required to balance the fund due to significant cost pressures such as Temporary Accommodation and net cost of housing benefit payments

news_drafts.headline: Lothbury property fund investment showing £0.826m realised loss with £0.953m total projected loss
news_drafts.lead: This shows capital risk on the council's non-treasury investments and that reserves are being consumed to cover losses on long-term holdings, reducing available reserves for service pressures.

news_drafts.headline: Council maintains £188.7m of under-borrowing (internal borrowing plus investments), creating refinancing risk if cash balances fall
news_drafts.lead: If the council's cash balance is drawn down by capital spending, deficit, or investment losses, it will be forced to external borrow at 3.41%+ rather than the 3.75% base rate it currently earns internally, creating budget pressure.

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme underspent by £82.9m (46%), creating future refinancing need for slipped schemes
news_drafts.lead: A lender needs to know the council can either complete the £82.9m of unspent capital schemes through internal cash without compromising liquidity, or will return to the market for external borrowing if cash is consumed elsewhere.
